items.stem: Which of the following best describes "exothermic reaction"?
options: An energy cycle for the formation of an ionic compound from its elements, used to calculate lattice enthalpy (HL)
The heat energy transferred between a system and its surroundings at constant pressure
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 K; for water 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹
A reaction that releases thermal energy to the surroundings; ΔH is negative and the surroundings get warmer
items.answer: A reaction that releases thermal energy to the surroundings; ΔH is negative and the surroundings get warmer
items.markingKey: D. "exothermic reaction" is a reaction that releases thermal energy to the surroundings; ΔH is negative and the surroundings get warmer.

items.stem: Leila writes: "A negative ΔH means the reaction will happen quickly." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: ΔH concerns energy change, not rate; rate depends on activation energy and conditions (e.g. diamond → graphite is exothermic but extremely slow).
items.markingKey: ΔH concerns energy change, not rate; rate depends on activation energy and conditions (e.g. diamond → graphite is exothermic but extremely slow). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between heat and temperature.
items.answer: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference (J); temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles (K).
items.markingKey: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference (J); temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles (K). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: On an energy profile, the reactants are at 150 kJ mol⁻¹, the transition state at 400 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products at 300 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
items.answer: 100 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: Ea(reverse) = H(TS) − H(products) = 400 − 300 = 100 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1); equivalently Ea(forward) − ΔH (M1).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Energy profiles give a complete description of a reaction."
items.answer: They are useful summaries of energetics but not of kinetics or spontaneity in full.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: show ΔH and Ea and the effect of catalysts; help predict whether heating is needed. Arguments against: give no information on rate constants, mechanism steps or entropy; are idealised one-dimensional plots of complex multi-dimensional changes. Supported judgement: They are useful summaries of energetics but not of kinetics or spontaneity in full.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The minimum energy that colliding particles need for a reaction to occur"?
items.answer: activation energy (Ea)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of activation energy (Ea).

items.stem: Which statement about a catalysed reaction is correct?
options: ΔH is unchanged but Ea is lower.
items.answer: ΔH is unchanged but Ea is lower.
items.markingKey: A. Catalysts provide an alternative pathway.

items.stem: Explain why most exothermic reactions still require an initial input of energy.
items.answer: Bonds in the reactants must first be broken (or particles must collide with energy ≥ Ea) to reach the transition state; energy released when new bonds form later exceeds that absorbed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Bonds in the reactants must first be broken (or particles must collide with energy ≥ Ea) to reach the transition state; energy released when new bonds form later exceeds that absorbed. items.stem: Jonas writes: "In an endothermic reaction the reaction mixture gets hot because energy is absorbed." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings, so the mixture and container feel colder.
items.markingKey: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings, so the mixture and container feel colder. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: On an energy profile, the reactants are at 200 kJ mol⁻¹, the transition state at 425 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products at 350 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for the forward reaction?
items.answer: +150 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: A. ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) = 350 − 200 = +150 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.answer: endothermic; ΔH positive; surroundings cool down
items.markingKey: A. Evaporation of sweat from skin is endothermic.

items.stem: Explain why ΔH is negative when the temperature of the water in a calorimeter rises.
items.answer: The heat gained by the water came from the reacting system, which therefore lost enthalpy; by convention heat released by the system gives a negative ΔH.

items.stem: Diego mixed 100.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ nitric acid with 100.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ potassium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rose by 3.2 K. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation per mole of water formed. (Assume the solution has a density of 1.00 g cm⁻³ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.)
items.answer: −53.5 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: B. q = mcΔT = 200 × 4.18 × 3.2 = 2680 J (M1); n(H₂O) = 0.0500 mol (M1); ΔH = −q/n = −53.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1, negative sign required).

items.stem: Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of C₂H₄(g): 2C(s) + 2H₂(g) → C₂H₄(g), using the enthalpies of combustion / kJ mol⁻¹: C(s) −394, H₂(g) −286, C₂H₄(g) −1411.
items.answer: +51.0 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΔHf = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) (M1) = 2(−394) + 2(−286) − (−1411) (M1) = +51.0 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem:
50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) was placed in a polystyrene cup and its temperature recorded every 30 s. At 90 s, 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at the same temperature was added. The thermometer reads to ±0.1 °C.

time / s | temperature / °C
0 | 21.1
30 | 21.1
60 | 21.1
90 | 25.1
120 | 27.9
150 | 27.6
180 | 27.2
210 | 26.8
240 | 26.4
270 | 26.1
300 | 25.7

(a) Explain why the maximum recorded temperature is not used directly to find ΔT. [1]
(b) By extrapolating the cooling section back to 90 s, determine the temperature change. [2]
(c) Calculate ΔH of neutralisation in kJ mol⁻¹. [2]
(d) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in ΔT. [2]
(e) State one assumption made in the calculation of q. [1]
items.answer: (a) Heat is lost to the surroundings while the mixture warms and after mixing; extrapolation corrects for this heat loss. (b) ΔT ≈ 7.2 K (c) −60.2 kJ mol⁻¹ (d) 2.8 % (e) The solution has the density (1.00 g cm⁻³) and specific heat capacity (4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹) of water / the cup absorbs no heat.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] Heat loss during the temperature rise (1). (b) [2] Extrapolated T at 90 s ≈ 28.3 °C (M1); ΔT = 28.3 − 21.1 = 7.2 K (A1). (c) [2] q = 100.0 × 4.18 × 7.2 = 3010 J (M1); n = 0.0500 mol; ΔH = −60.2 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1). (d) [2] ±0.2 K (two readings) / 7.2 × 100 (M1) = 2.8 % (A1). (e) [1] Any valid assumption (1).

items.stem: Estimate the enthalpy change for the reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g) using the bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) in the data booklet.
items.answer: −482 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: bonds broken = 2 × H–H (436) + O=O (498) = 1370 kJ (M1); bonds formed = 4 × O–H (463) = 1852 kJ (M1); ΔH = 1370 − 1852 = −482 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Coffee-cup calorimetry gives accurate values for enthalpies of reaction."
items.answer: Useful for comparison and teaching; for accurate data bomb calorimetry and careful corrections are needed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: simple and quick; good for reactions in solution; results with neutralisation are often within 5 % of literature. Arguments against: heat loss to surroundings and cup; assumes density and specific heat capacity of solution equal water; thermometer resolution limits precision for small ΔT. Supported judgement: Useful for comparison and teaching; for accurate data bomb calorimetry and careful corrections are needed.

items.stem: "Energy profiles give a complete description of a reaction." Discuss.
items.answer: They are useful summaries of energetics but not of kinetics or spontaneity in full.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: show ΔH and Ea and the effect of catalysts; help predict whether heating is needed. Arguments against: give no information on rate constants, mechanism steps or entropy; are idealised one-dimensional plots of complex multi-dimensional changes. Supported judgement: They are useful summaries of energetics but not of kinetics or spontaneity in full. items.stem: For C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g): (a) calculate ΔH using average bond enthalpies; (b) calculate ΔH using ΔHf⦵ values (CO₂(g) −394, H₂O(g) −242, CH₄(g) −74, C₃H₈(g) −105 kJ mol⁻¹); (c) explain why the two values differ; (d) state which value is more reliable.
items.answer: (a) −2030 kJ mol⁻¹; (b) −2040 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) broken − formed = −2030 kJ mol⁻¹ (M1 A1). (b) ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = −2040 kJ mol⁻¹ (M1 A1). (c) bond enthalpies are averages from many compounds, not specific to these molecules (R1). (d) ΔHf value – based on measured data for the actual substances (R1).
